lines.text: It's three in the morning, and you're slicing a bagel in the hospital break room. The knife slips.
Half an inch of your finger is just... gone.
You're a doctor. You know exactly what to do. Ice, gauze, call the surgeon. But before you can move, your finger starts to itch.
Then it grows. Bone, then skin, then a tiny new nail. Forty seconds. Not even a scar.
The night nurse drops her coffee. You drop the bagel.
So what if you could regrow any part of your body?
Sounds impossible? Not for everyone. An axolotl, a smiling little salamander from Mexico, can regrow a leg, part of its heart, even pieces of its brain. Without a single scar.
In eighteen ninety-eight, scientist Thomas Hunt Morgan cut a flatworm into tiny pieces. A piece just one two-hundred-seventy-ninth of the worm grew into a whole new worm.
Today, that's you. Only you're a doctor.
First, you need to know how it works. So you do what any scientist would do. You experiment on yourself.
Your colleague, Dr. Reyes, takes a tiny slice of skin from your arm, then stitches the wound shut, nice and neat.
Nothing happens. A week later, you just have a scar.
So she takes another slice, and this time leaves the wound open under a bandage. Twenty seconds later, the skin is back.
Rule number one: a stitched wound scars. An open one regrows.

Weirdly, real doctors noticed something similar. In nineteen seventy-four, Dr. Cynthia Illingworth in Sheffield reported that children's cut-off fingertips often grew back, if surgeons just left them alone instead of stitching them closed.
It works in kids up to about eleven years old. Nail, fingerprint and all.
Rule number two shows up at lunch. You're starving. You eat two burgers, a pizza, and half the vending machine.
A new body part has to be built from something, and that something is whatever you eat. Every regrowth costs you a mountain of food.
Rule number three shows up at a softball game. A ball knocks out your front tooth. By dinner, a new one has pushed in.
Not a copy of the old tooth. A brand-new one. No filling, no stains. Whatever regrows comes back factory new.

Real scientists are chasing this exact trick. In twenty twenty-four, doctors in Kyoto began the first human trial of a drug meant to help people grow new teeth. They hope it could reach patients around twenty thirty.
Now, a doctor who can regrow anything starts asking a dangerous question. What else could I give away?
Here's a real fact: the human liver regrows. A living donor can give part of theirs to a patient, and in about two months it grows back to almost full size.
Yours grows back overnight.
So you become a donor. A slice of liver in March. Another in April. By December, you've given away more than one whole liver, and you're still using yours.
Then you try a kidney. A normal kidney can't regrow at all. Yours is back in four days.
The waiting list at your hospital gets shorter every week. The newspapers call you "the Spare Parts Doctor."
And companies come calling. A man in a very expensive suit offers you a billion dollars for a vial of your cells.
Real labs are already trying to grow body parts. In two thousand six, Dr. Anthony Atala reported seven young patients living with bladders grown from their own cells.
And in twenty twenty-two, a young woman in Texas received an ear that was 3D-printed from her own cartilage cells.
But real labs are slow, and you're not. You turn down the man in the suit. You've got patients waiting.
Then, one Tuesday, Dr. Reyes looks at your blood test and goes quiet.
Your cells are dividing faster than anything she's ever seen. Faster than a deer antler.
Antlers are one of the fastest-growing tissues of any mammal. Up to two centimeters a day.
And in twenty nineteen, scientists found that antlers grow using genes that look a lot like the genes of bone cancer. The deer just know how to keep them in check.
Fast growth and cancer are two sides of the same coin. In nineteen eighty-six, a doctor named Harold Dvorak described tumors as "wounds that do not heal."
"Every time you regrow something," Reyes says, "you roll the dice."
You start counting. Forty-one regrowths. Forty-one rolls of the dice.
Three weeks later, you find it. A small, hard lump on your forearm, right where that second slice of skin grew back.
Your hands shake while Reyes cuts it out. It isn't cancer. Not yet. It's just skin that didn't know when to stop.
This time, she stitches the wound shut. On purpose. A scar is a stop sign.
Maybe that's why we scar at all. One theory says mammals traded regrowing for something faster and safer: a quick patch that stops infection, and keeps runaway growth in check.
So you decide to stop. No more regrowing. Ever.
And that's exactly when Lily arrives. She's seven. Her liver is failing, and there's no donor for her on the list.
Except you. Same blood type. A perfect match.
A normal donor would grow that piece back over a couple of months. You'll grow it back in one night. Another roll of the dice.
Reyes sits down next to you in the empty cafeteria. "You don't owe anyone this," she says.
You look at the bagel on your tray. The same kind that started all of this.
Then you sign the form.
The surgery takes nine hours. By morning, Lily's new liver is working. And yours has already grown back.
For a week, you check your skin every morning. No lumps. The counter stops at forty-two. And that's where you leave it.
Here's the twist, though. You don't need a superpower to regrow body parts. You already can. A little.
Your liver regrows. Your skin keeps replacing itself. A broken bone rebuilds itself, and a rib can even grow back, if surgeons leave its outer lining in place.
Cut nerves regrow too, about a millimeter a day. And kids' fingertips grow back, if we just leave them alone.
The power isn't missing. It's switched off. And scientists are looking for the switch.

In twenty twenty-two, a team led by Michael Levin at Tufts University put a tiny dome filled with five drugs over a frog's cut leg, for just twenty-four hours. Over the next eighteen months, the frog regrew a working leg.
It wasn't perfect. But a frog that shouldn't regrow a leg did. And mammals are next on the list.
A year later, Lily is back in your ER. She caught her finger in a car door. The tip is gone.
The surgeon on duty reaches for the needle and thread. You stop him. "Leave it open. Just a dressing."
Eight weeks later, Lily shows you a brand-new fingertip. Nail and all. No superpower needed.
So if you could regrow one body part, which one would you pick? Tell me in the comments.
And subscribe.
